name: Software Defined Radio

claims.claim_text: The defining split is an analog front end with everything after it done digitally, which is what allows filtering, demodulation and mixing to be changed without touching hardware — one board becomes many radios through a recompile.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have an analog front end and then you do everything else digitally
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Bob Pease, Jim Williams - Posthumous Pease Porridge

claims.claim_text: Rather than fixing the local oscillator in hardware, the mixing frequency is left as an input and supplied digitally, which is what makes frequency-hopping schemes such as cellular practical to implement and change on the fly.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to pipe in some kind of mixing frequency basically you leave that hanging and then you pipe that in digitally
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Bob Pease, Jim Williams - Posthumous Pease Porridge

claims.claim_text: Direct-conversion architecture removes the front-end amplifier and often the front-end bandpass filter entirely, which eliminates the insertion loss those stages contribute.
claims.quote_verbatim: software-defined radio, you don't have to have a front-end amplifier at all. Sometimes you don't even need to have a front-end bandpass filter
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Converting straight from RF to a very low intermediate frequency moves the whole signal chain into territory served by ordinary op-amps and instrumentation amplifiers, with filtering done in plain resistors and capacitors — cheaper parts and far less power than an RF chain, with the cost shifted to whether the processor can keep up after digitisation.
claims.quote_verbatim: you go directly from RF down to a very low intermediate frequency. So that means that you're using amplifiers, which are just off-the-shelf op-amps and instrumentation amplifiers that work in the kilohertz range
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: The conventional implementation stack is an integrated RF transceiver chip, an FPGA-plus-ARM device to absorb the sample stream, and a Linux host doing the higher-level processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: your typical SDR setup with one of those analog devices chips. Then a Zinc to take all the data in. And then, then we process that on a Linux computer
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Modern cellular base stations split the radio physically: the software-defined radio sits as a radio head mounted at the antenna, connected by fibre to a baseband unit that handles the protocol, so only encoded data travels the long path.
claims.quote_verbatim: in modern cell networks, you will have a, what's called the radio head, which is basically the software defined radio that you're going to Mount near the antenna
claims.speaker: Sylvain Minot
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: Digitising close to the antenna with little or no analog filtering makes a receiver acutely vulnerable to out-of-band interference: a strong signal well away from the wanted one overloads the converter and jams the receiver, which is a measurable regression against 1980s and 1990s receiver front ends.
claims.quote_verbatim: that whole architecture of going RF antenna to A to D with no analog filtering or minimal analog filtering means that those radios are extremely sensitive to things like out-of-band interference
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: It's a Keyzermas Miracle!

claims.claim_text: The trade made across the whole consumer radio industry was integration, power and cost against front-end robustness, and it was made on the buyer's behalf rather than offered as a choice.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have made the compromise that they've gotten better integration, lower power, lower cost, and they do as much digital processing in silicon as they can
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: It's a Keyzermas Miracle!

claims.claim_text: Transmit is where the architecture strains: a power amplifier that stays efficient across a broad frequency range is genuinely hard, exactly as broadband antennas are, so the agility the digital side promises is limited by the analog output stage.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the major weaknesses of software defined radios is on the transmitting side and making RF power amplifiers that are agile in frequency is very hard
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: Receiving is forgiving of an incomplete grasp of RF — the result is merely worse sensitivity — while transmitting without understanding what the hardware is emitting has regulatory consequences, so the two sides of the same board carry very different risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're still going to be able to receive just, yeah, maybe not as well. Or especially you definitely don't want to be transmitting without having some sense of what you're doing
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: The power budget rules the architecture out of battery-powered devices outright; the everyday evidence is that a laptop's fans spin up as soon as an SDR is running on it.
claims.quote_verbatim: cannot do SDR for power budget reasons
claims.speaker: Travis Goodspeed
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: Using an SDR in a system that also transmits runs into timing and synchronisation as the hard problem, because the platforms are built for continuous streaming rather than for holding a deterministic relationship with an external transmitter.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's timing, it's synchronization. It's how do you synchronize your transmitter with the software to find, uh, radio. They're meant for streaming applications
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Greg Charvat Returns With A Book! - Laboratory Literature Laureate

claims.claim_text: A half-duplex transceiver cannot both transmit and receive at once, so a radar-style application needs either two units with their clocks synchronised or a small add-on board carrying the transmit chirp generator alongside a single SDR.
claims.quote_verbatim: the obvious way is to use two HackRFs since it's a, a, uh, half duplex transceiver
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Very low transmit power still reaches long range through pulse compression: send long linear-FM pulses and recover range resolution in the Fourier transform, which is precisely the kind of processing software-defined techniques make available cheaply.
claims.quote_verbatim: they use pulse compression. They use linear FM and they use the 4A transform. They send long pulses
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: A software-defined radio solves the modulation problem and nothing else: it gets bits in and bits out, leaving routing, store-and-forward, the application layer and everything that makes the data useful still to be built — which is why large radio products carry whole teams downstream of the radio itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: just solve one part of the problem. That's the, like really just the modulation
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: When the requirement is a known modulation at tens to hundreds of kilobits, a fixed-function radio chip is the right answer: choosing flexibility you do not need spends the whole schedule re-solving modulation instead of on the part of the problem that is actually unsolved.
claims.quote_verbatim: just need a GMSK or something that basically can get tens to hundreds of kilobits
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: Much low-speed digital RF work — remote keyless entry, garage doors, smart meters, home automation, industrial control — is better served by a wireless microcontroller on a USB dongle than by an SDR, and conflating the two leads people to reach for far more capability than the job needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: the number one thing I have to tell people about Yardstick 1 is it's not software-defined radio
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Building an SDR from scratch is not a short project; starting from a plug-in board for an existing digital platform avoids laying out a 600-pin BGA FPGA to get to the same experiment.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you started your own, you know, software defined radio from scratch, you're not going to get it done in two months
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: Implementing the signal processing in FPGA logic is the harder path — the algorithms are tricky and iteration in C is far faster than in Verilog — so a good platform is heterogeneous, offering an application processor, FPGA fabric and a parallel processor array so each piece of the chain lands where it is cheapest to develop.
claims.quote_verbatim: not everybody wants to do an SDR in FPGA logic. It's just, it's just hard
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Spectrum analysis and demodulation of common signals — broadcast FM, land mobile and public safety radio in both analog and digital form, and the standard amateur modes — are available from existing applications with no code written; the framework only becomes necessary beyond that.
claims.quote_verbatim: can do some things without code, like spectrum analysis and demodulation of common things like FM radio stations
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: GNU Radio is the recommended framework for anything beyond the prepackaged applications, and it accepts either C++ or Python, so the language is not a barrier to entry.
claims.quote_verbatim: radio is the framework that I recommend people use
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: In the graphical companion the radio appears as a source block emitting a stream of samples, and processing is assembled by dragging in blocks — from an addition of two signals up to a complete cellular receiver — which is what turns signal processing into something composable rather than something written from scratch.
claims.quote_verbatim: i stream this data into gnu radio which is this framework and i end up with just a radio source block
claims.speaker: Derek Kozel
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: Frequency-domain analysis is computationally expensive but heavily optimised: a Fourier transform can be run over several hundred million samples per second, particularly with a graphics card doing the work, and the data is streamed and discarded rather than stored.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can pretty much do that to you know several hundred uh million samples per second especially if you start throwing a graphics card at it
claims.speaker: Derek Kozel
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: Documentation that exists but is not surfaced inside the tool goes unused: a lead on the project itself had not built the habit of consulting it after two years, because it was not present in the graphical environment where the work happens.
claims.quote_verbatim: gnu radio has a huge amount of documentation that even after two years of me using it i haven't built the habit of accessing it because it's not right
claims.speaker: Derek Kozel
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: Driving an SDR as a spectrum analyser through rapid sweeping is mostly a host-software problem with some device firmware behind it, rather than a different radio — the same hardware becomes a survey instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: using a software defined radio platform more like a spectrum analyzer
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Conning with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: The cheap television-tuner dongles are receive-only with a narrower tuning range than a purpose-built platform, but they run the same host software, so the low-cost path is a genuine subset rather than a separate ecosystem.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're receive only, whereas HackRF can also transmit. And they have a more limited operating frequency range
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: A purpose-built low-cost receiver project — an ARM with an external converter and a television tuner — was made irrelevant by the repurposed twenty-dollar dongle: the deliberate design had the better receiver, but the price-performance ratio was not close.
claims.quote_verbatim: that kind of made the Osmo SDR project a little bit irrelevant because there was no way we were going to compete in price
claims.speaker: Sylvain Minot
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: An open transmit-capable platform of that generation covered 30 MHz to 6 GHz for about $275, which is the point where building an equivalent yourself stops being economic.
claims.quote_verbatim: it goes from 30 you can uh transmit or receive anything from 30 megahertz to 6 gig
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hyperloop, Upverter and Soldering - Unbelievable USB Ustulater

claims.claim_text: An early low-cost receiver covering roughly 150 MHz to 1.3 GHz for around $200 was general-purpose in the sense that matters: the modulation format is irrelevant to the hardware as long as a decoder exists in software, which is what let people pull weather-satellite imagery off the same board built for a student satellite downlink.
claims.quote_verbatim: a radio that can tune in any frequency from, it's like 150 megahertz up to 1.3 gigahertz
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Horrisonous Holiday Habromania

claims.claim_text: The design goal for a general-purpose platform was explicitly not to be the best tool for any single job but to be usable across many, which is the deliberate opposite of how a purpose-built radio is specified.
claims.quote_verbatim: don't see HackerRF being the best tool for any one job, but it's a great tool that can be used for a huge variety of jobs
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: A cheap dongle plus a spectrum display makes filtering and bandwidth concrete in a way that working the mathematics alone does not — seeing that a filter is narrowing onto the region where the signal actually sits is the shift that a signals course usually fails to deliver.
claims.quote_verbatim: looking at a spectrum and realizing that when you're doing a filter, you're just narrowing in on like this little part that's darker where the signal actually is
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: Toggling a pin from a shift register at a chosen rate while watching the result on an SDR builds an intuition for what a circuit radiates — the fastest way to develop a feel for both intentional transmission and the unintentional emissions coming off the traces on a board.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you just generally like write some code to turn it up in on and off at a certain speed using like a strip register and you have a software defined radio and you're looking at the signal
claims.speaker: CNLohr
claims.episode_title: Long Distance with CNLohr-a

claims.claim_text: The first open HDTV receiver was built by recording samples off the air and post-processing them to MPEG rather than in real time, on a $1,500 data acquisition card paired with an evaluation board from a cancelled product line — the hardware gap, not the software, was what limited early work.
claims.quote_verbatim: that was done with a $1,500 data acquisition card and a TV tuner evaluation board from a company that had actually already gone out
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Wide bandwidth, MIMO and FPGA-side signal processing had no path below tens of thousands of dollars, and the USRP began as a block diagram drawn by someone who wanted to use such a thing and could not persuade anyone else to build it.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was no practical way to do that for less than tens of thousands of dollars
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Low-cost transmit-capable hardware did not exist fifteen years ago, which is why end-to-end tutorials remain scarce relative to receive-only material — the teaching lags the hardware availability rather than the theory.
claims.quote_verbatim: transmit capable low cost uh sdrs were totally non-existent 15 years ago
claims.speaker: Derek Kozel
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: The strongest product argument is post-deployment change: with every ground device a software-defined radio, the waveform, congestion control and transmission scheduling can all be reconfigured on units already in the field.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're all software defined radios. So if you want to change the waveform or change how to, how the system integrates or how the congestion control is done
claims.speaker: Maarten Engelen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Maarten Engelen

claims.claim_text: Regulators require equipment going through authorisation to implement a mechanism stopping the user from altering the radio's parameters, a requirement that cannot be met and be open source at the same time; the same rule was later extended from SDR products to any radio under software control, which is what brought it to the attention of people reflashing wireless routers.
claims.quote_verbatim: they wanted software-defined radios that were going through equipment authorization. They wanted them to implement some kind of security measure to prevent users from modifying the radio parameters
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Any unencrypted link should be designed on the assumption that it is being captured, because standing up a receiver to record the traffic is now cheap; what protects most low-value links is that nobody considers the contents worth the effort.
claims.quote_verbatim: could set up an SDR and you could just capture all this traffic too
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Watt Is The Deal

claims.claim_text: Cellular and combination wireless chips are already software-defined radios internally, so the practical integration limits sit in the multiplexing and the antenna — whether a recommended cellular antenna is wideband enough to be useful at 2.4 GHz as well — rather than in the radio itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: internal of these chips, like they're all SDRs internally
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: The technology did not make RF engineers obsolete, it changed the problems they solve: a general-purpose SDR schematic is full of switches, up and down converters and mixers, and someone has to get all of it right.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you look at the HackRF, there's a ton of RF circuitry in there. I mean, I was poking around in the schematics a couple of weeks ago and there are switches and up converters, down converters, mixers
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: Published receiver code exists for the public pager networks, where the wide-area systems use FLEX and short-range applications such as restaurant pagers use POCSAG — a useful reminder that legacy unencrypted protocols remain in daily service.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are people who, um, have published like software defined radio code to sniff the public pager networks
claims.speaker: Travis Goodspeed
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep101 labels the guest's entire career and USRP origin story as 'Chris Gammell'; the content is unambiguously Matt Ettus and is attributed to him.

ep265, ep318 and ep352 similarly label Michael Ossmann's first-person material (his NTIA work, the HackRF and Jawbreaker projects, his classes) as the hosts; those claims are content-attributed to Michael Ossmann.
ep381 labels Derek Kozel's answers as 'Chris Gammell'; the GNU Radio and Ettus Research material is content-attributed to Derek Kozel.
ep427 labels the Hiber guest's description of his own system as 'Dave Jones'; content-attributed to Maarten Engelen.
ep401 could not be resolved between the two Salmi brothers who appear as a single speaker label, so those claims carry speaker: null.
Host sentiment and audience-response material — enthusiasm for particular products, Kickstarter totals, conference travel and who bought what — was excluded.
